Brown Locusts

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Unprecedented rainfall across the country has brought not only relief for our farmers... but also millions of brown locusts!

Unique Selling Point:
Swarms of brown locusts have been reported across the Eastern and Northern Cape - across the Karoo. And they're munching their way through farmers' crops and grazing. The swarms are said to travel up to 100kms in a single day and are massive, containing hundreds of thousands of individuals. Farmers speak of swarms that span a kilometre, eating EVERYTHING in sight. The Government is in charge of control, but because of the nature of the insecticide used, houses cannot be treated, so people are suffering. Dead locusts, left to rot are smelly and an eyesore in some smaller towns.

Summary:
Farmers are crying, they have spent the last years battling a drought and now that they finally have grazing for their livestock, that could be wiped out overnight by a single swarm of brown locusts.

And a bigger threat looms for the adjacent provinces. If the swarms migrate to our crop intensive areas (Northwest or Free State) they could have a massive impact on our food production and cause huge problems for the agricultural sector.

On average we have large outbreaks in SA between 7 to 11 years. The locusts live for about 78 days and a single female lays 380 eggs.
Problems we have these days is that the Karoo has changed over the last few decades. A lot of land is being farmed remotely, which means there is no-one on the land and there is a break in surveilance. Increased security on farms also means that pest control teams don’t have easy access to land…

Further information:
The summer rains have wreaked havoc for farmers. 60% of crops in the Western Freestate are said to fail because of too much rain or hail. And it’s too late to replant. Same happening in Eastern Freestate where maize farmers are reporting fungus in their crops because the maize and wheat is literally standing in swamps. Also means farmers cannot get into the fields to remove weeds and do pest control. In some places wheat is ready to be harvested but they cannot get into the fields.

According to the Agricultural Pests Act, Government is responsible for the management of Brown Locust outbreaks. And generally they do a good job, — the only thing farmers can do themselves is crush the hoppers before they fly. The locusts are high in fat and a good source of protein so sheep can feed on them, and technically humans too… but there are too many locusts and too few people to control the outbreak.

Biggest problem we have is monitoring the swarms. They can travel up to 100km a day.
UN Food and Agriculture Organisation has a good model where they track pests with satellite technology and drones. We should have something similar, but we don’t.

The Karoo Brown Locust is a medium-sized insect from the genus Locustana. It is native to the arid Karoo and especially adapted for this dry region. Eggs have an impermeable cuticle to protect them and they can lie in the ground, unhatched for years… waiting for the conditions to be perfect!

According to records, there are outbreaks reported as far back as 1797… and 2022 seems to be their lucky year! Swarms have been reported across the Eastern and Northern Cape - across the Karoo. The last major outbreak was in 1985-86 and ended up costing the country about R50 million. It takes a lot of labour and costly chemicals to destroy a swarm.

Agri chemical and -pest specialist, Dr Gerhard Verdoorn says at the moment the Karoo vegetation is quite abundant thanks to the rains. This means that the veld is full of food for the critters. But they cannot be left… They could move to other areas in the country where they can do a lot more damage and they do pose a threat to road safety. When you drive through a swarm your windscreen will be covered in a thick fatty goo — making visibility difficult, which could cause problems, especially on smaller roads.




Extra Budget Items:
Travel to Hopetown area
Accommodation for the Crew for 2 nights
Will need presenter for an extra day as it is far

Press Release:


Hoppers of Biblical Proportions
Persistent rainfall has transformed the usually arid Northern Cape and Karoo into a lush, green landscape. But it has also brought a two-year-long plague of brown locusts. Native to the Karoo and Southern Namibia, these hungry hoppers have been hatching in swarms dense enough to eclipse the sun and lay waste to entire crops. Carte Blanche takes to the road to track down a swarm and witness the effects of the onslaught ourselves.
Producer: Stenette Grosskopf | Presenter: Claire Mawisa

Script:


BROWN LOCUSTS - SCRIPT
V/O
Above average rainfall across large parts of South Africa means that many landscapes have changed…

In some areas crops are literally drowning in swamps, and for the first time in years the Karoo is lush… almost unrecognizable….
LINK
When we’ve come to this part of the world as Carte Blanche - The Free State and the Northern Cape, we’ve always brought you stories about the drought… but this time it’s a completely different story…
V/O
We’re on our way to the Hopetown district on the edge of the Great Karoo … – locust hunting…
UPSOUNDS
They manufacture potholes in Koffiefontein…
V/O
For almost two years the area has been plagued by massive swarms of brown locusts… and everyone you meet along the way has photos to share and a story to tell….
UPSOUND
Sover as ek kan kyk…
Dile UPSOUND
Het jy al ‘n springkaan in jou bed gekry?

Ja mevrou. As ek daar lê, krap hy my hier…
V/O
Since the start of the summer, farmers report that locust numbers have grown exponentially…

And they eat everything in sight as they move through the veld.
UPSOUND VIDEO
Dis rooi-briun van die massas…
V/O
There are plenty of photos and videos on social media, but we want to see the locusts ourselves and we’re told this area, just about 20kms from the Orange River, is brimming with locusts.

There’s just one little problem… RAIN
LINK
Finding the locusts is one thing, but getting to them is a whole other story. These unrelenting rains have made the roads muddy and they are all flooded, and it’s not just because we’re city slickers – the farmers themselves are finding these roads difficult to navigate…
Riaan Badenhorst
Ons het tussen 200 en 300mm reenval al gehad van Novembermaand af waar ons gemiddelde reenval is 400mm in ‘n jaar!
V/O
Here they have had more than half their annual rainfall in a matter of months… and their official raining season is yet to come!
V/O
Sheep farmer, Riaan Badenhorst was all set to take us to the locusts, but with all the mud and slippery roads the trip is impossible today… And although we’re disappointed, I get the idea that Riaan is a bit relieved…
Riaan Badenhorst
Ek is nou al gatvol vir ‘n springkaan… Jy ry dalk by hulle verby of jy sien dalk op die TV ‘n swerm springkane dan het jy so ‘n idee, maar as hulle gaan slaap in die aand dan lê hulle partykeer op ‘n 4, 500ha.

As jy stop en die bakkie se geluid afgaan, die enjin… dan hoor jy tjir tjir tjir soos hulle eet.
V/O
Riaan says this is the biggest outbreak of Karoo Brown Locusts he’s seen in his 57 years on the farm.
Riaan Badenhorst
Dit is maar net die toestande en omstandighede wat 100% is vir hulle om uit te broei. En meer as een generasie in ‘n seisoen!
Willem Symington
The Northern Cape has always had outbreaks of locusts. It's a natural occurrence, if we get good summer rains, then we get outbreaks of locusts.


V/O
Willem Symington, Agri SA's Chairman of the Natural Resources Centre of Excellence, farms in the Williston District. He drove out to meet us in De Aar…
Willem Symington
Claire: Can you give us a visual understanding of where and how much these locusts are. …
Put yourself in this situation and try and imagine what it's like in swarms that are kilometers wide and kilometers long and overhead the sun darkens. It's like an eclipse of the Sun.
UPSOUND VIDEO


V/O
The Brown Locust is native to the Karoo and Southern Namibia and is actually a fascinating insect.
PROF HOLM


Hierdie is die doodgewone, groen-bruin veld springkaan wat as hulle mekaar te dikwels ontmoet as hoppers, dan slaan hulle oor na ‘n ander genetika, en dan lees hulle ‘n ander boek, as’t ware.
V/O
Veteran entomologist, Professor Erik Holm spent many years documenting the brown locusts in the Karoo. He says it was his predecessor at the University of Pretoria, JC Faure, who uncovered some of the mysteries of the locusts in the 1920’s…
PROF HOLM


Tot daar was hulle in al die museums as twee genera, verskillende - nie net spesies nie, verskillende genera geklassifiseer – die enkel fase, en die swerm fase…
V/O
And even though they are the same species, they don’t just behave differently, they also look very different.
PROF HOLM
Dis die alleenloper fase - bleek en dan word hy groen. En dis die swerm fase - rooi en dan word hy swart en rooi - baie opvallende kleure, ne?
V/O
And they are very well-adapted to the dry climate, with eggs lying dormant in the soil for years, waiting for rains like this…

But despite being a natural phenomenon, millions of hungry grasshoppers munching their way through the Karoo is not ideal for the farmers.
Willem Symington
In a perfect world? We would like nature to take its course. But human beings, we've already altered nature and the processes in nature to such an extent that for our survival, we've got to manage nature..
V/O
For the farmers, controlling the locusts is about much more than just protecting grazing for their livestock…
Riaan Badenhorst
Hulle vreet ‘n mielieland op, hulle vreet ‘n sojaboonland op. En daai stapel is daarmee heen.
Willem Symington
Can you imagine what would happen if all these swarms goes into your crop growing areas in the Free State? What? It's going to be a real disaster.
Claire: So then how does it work in terms of trying to control these locust swarms and populations?
The government provides the pesticide, the training for the people to control the locals and equipment in the point people out of the local communities.
V/O
The Northern Cape is divided into 52 agricultural districts, and a District Locust Officer is appointed for each region. Riaan Badenhorst looks after the Hopetown district, where he has 10 teams working under him, spraying swarms almost 7 days a week.
Riaan Badenhorst
Die vlieërs spuit ons net in die nag, want hulle vlieg deur die dag. En hulle vlieg party aande tot 8 uur in die aand vlieg hulle nog.
V/O
The adult locusts can travel over 60kms a day, but when it gets dark, they huddle together… and that’s when the teams move in with the pesticide.
Riaan Badenhorst
Soos wat hulle nou is, is ‘n mens maar elke aand besig, en elke oggend vroegoggend besig met hulle. So hulle vat maar ‘n bietjie van jou tyd. Maar dit is mos maar een van die opofferings wat mens maak as jy ‘n veeboer is en jy wil jou veld oppas…
V/O
The amount of pesticide they use is staggering. Riaan says he uses about 10 to 12, 200 liter drums of chemicals per week!
The pesticides are distributed from 2 depots in the Northern Cape - one in Upington, and the other one, here in De Aar.
Willem Symington
Claire: So when we’re talking about the actual pesticide, is it environmentally friendly, I mean we’re talking about 100s of liters being sprayed across the veld. Is it going to do any lasting damage, or no?
Willem, In previous years when we still worked with organophosphates, that was really harmful to the environment, … but it’s new pesticide. It’s registered only for locusts, it’s very specie specific, it does no further harm to the environment…
LINK
It’s hard to imagine that right now there are millions of locusts swarming this part of the country. We’ve been here for 2 days and have traveled a thousand kilometres and have not spotted a single one yet. And that is why they are so difficult to control and with the veld looking this lush there could be a swarm just on the other side of this pond and no-one would notice.
Riaan Badenhorst
Baie boere is nie op die plase self nie. Daar’s niemand op die plase nie. 90% van die sprinkane wat gerapporteer word is op ‘n pad, so die ouens ry oor die sprinkane en dan sien hulle hul toevallig.
V/o
Our Locust hunting trip is fast coming to an end, but in a last-ditch attempt to see the hoppers, we head to Strydenburg where some locusts were spotted earlier today.
But as luck would have it, we drive into a massive swarm on the road…
UPSOUND CLAIRE
We’ve got locusts!
V/O
But catching them is no easy task!
UPSOUND CLAIRE
Out of my hands!
V/O
Luckily we were forward thinking…
CLAIRE LINK
Guys I don’t know… I’ve been on a hunt for many things in my life but I feel like I’ve won the jackpot by finding these little locusts.. We’ve been looking for you for so long… These are tiny and we were just driving on the road and finally we saw millions of them… they look like dust…
V/O
In Strydenburg, local District Locust Officer, Johannes van der Merwe takes us to another swarm of newly hatched hoppers…
Johannes van der Merwe
Kyk hoe kom hulle af hierso in die pad…
V/O
We tell Johannes about the swarm we just encountered outside the town. If the rain stays away he will go look for them once the sun sets…
Johannes van der Merwe
Hier is duidelik ‘n krises aan die kom want hulle broei uit soos julle nou kan sien…
Willem Symington
Claire: Would you choose locusts over the drought?
I will always use locusts over the drought because if the two have locusts, you have to have some rain, and the locust is not going to eat up all the grazing.


Riaan Badenhorst
Ons sal liewerste maar met hulle baklei voor ons weer ‘n droogte vat….
V/O
The sun sets as we head back to Johannesburg … past the maize growing in dams of water … and one cannot help but wonder to what extent all this is because of OUR mistreatment of nature…




*********






PROMO 1 21’
Claire Link: I’m in the Northern Cape and it’s like you’ve never seen it before. It’s green, it’s lush. For the most part the farmers are happy… except for one little problem.. Wait.. make that a million little problems.
Upsound Willem: Overhead the sun darkens.
Upsound Riaan: Dis nou een van die plae van die bybel nog wat regtig ‘n plaag is…
PROMO 2 21”
Millions of hoppers, munching their way through the Karoo veld…
UPSOUND Willem: They eat everything…
UPSOUND Riaan: As jy hulle moet los dan sal dit katastrofiese gevolge hê.
UPSOUND Willem: Can you imagine what would happen of all these swarms goes into your crop growing areas…
We travel to the Great Karoo in search of locusts…
PROMO 3 11”
UPSOUND: Day two of our road trip and it has not stopped raining! Wonderful for the farmers, but not so good for hunting locusts…

V/O Riaan says this is the biggest outbreak of Karoo Brown Locusts he’s seen in his 57 years on the farm. Riaan Badenhorst Dit is maar net die toestande en omstandighede wat 100% is vir hulle om uit te broei. En meer as een generasie in ‘n seisoen! Willem Symington The Northern Cape has always had outbreaks of locusts. It's a natural occurrence, if we get good summer rains, then we get outbreaks of locusts. V/O Willem Symington, Agri SA's Chairman of the Natural Resources Centre of Excellence, farms in the Williston District. He drove out to meet us in De Aar… Willem Symington Claire: Can you give us a visual understanding of where and how much these locusts are. … Put yourself in this situation and try and imagine what it's like in swarms that are kilometers wide and kilometers long and overhead the sun darkens. It's like an eclipse of the Sun. UPSOUND VIDEO V/O The Brown Locust is native to the Karoo and Southern Namibia and is actually a fascinating insect. PROF HOLM Hierdie is die doodgewone, groen-bruin veld springkaan wat as hulle mekaar te dikwels ontmoet as hoppers, dan slaan hulle oor na ‘n ander genetika, en dan lees hulle ‘n ander boek, as’t ware. V/O Veteran entomologist, Professor Erik Holm spent many years documenting the brown locusts in the Karoo. He says it was his predecessor at the University of Pretoria, JC Faure, who uncovered some of the mysteries of the locusts in the 1920’s… PROF HOLM Tot daar was hulle in al die museums as twee genera, verskillende - nie net spesies nie, verskillende genera geklassifiseer – die enkel fase, en die swerm fase… V/O And even though they are the same species, they don’t just behave differently, they also look very different. PROF HOLM Dis die alleenloper fase - bleek en dan word hy groen. En dis die swerm fase - rooi en dan word hy swart en rooi - baie opvallende kleure, ne? V/O And they are very well-adapted to the dry climate, with eggs lying dormant in the soil for years, waiting for rains like this… But despite being a natural phenomenon, millions of hungry grasshoppers munching their way through the Karoo is not ideal for the farmers. Willem Symington In a perfect world? We would like nature to take its course. But human beings, we've already altered nature and the processes in nature to such an extent that for our survival, we've got to manage nature.. V/O For the farmers, controlling the locusts is about much more than just protecting grazing for their livestock… Riaan Badenhorst Hulle vreet ‘n mielieland op, hulle vreet ‘n sojaboonland op. En daai stapel is daarmee heen. Willem Symington Can you imagine what would happen if all these swarms goes into your crop growing areas in the Free State? What? It's going to be a real disaster. Claire: So then how does it work in terms of trying to control these locust swarms and populations? The government provides the pesticide, the training for the people to control the locals and equipment in the point people out of the local communities. V/O The Northern Cape is divided into 52 agricultural districts, and a District Locust Officer is appointed for each region. Riaan Badenhorst looks after the Hopetown district, where he has 10 teams working under him, spraying swarms almost 7 days a week. Riaan Badenhorst Die vlieërs spuit ons net in die nag, want hulle vlieg deur die dag. En hulle vlieg party aande tot 8 uur in die aand vlieg hulle nog. V/O The adult locusts can travel over 60kms a day, but when it gets dark, they huddle together… and that’s when the teams move in with the pesticide. Riaan Badenhorst Soos wat hulle nou is, is ‘n mens maar elke aand besig, en elke oggend vroegoggend besig met hulle. So hulle vat maar ‘n bietjie van jou tyd. Maar dit is mos maar een van die opofferings wat mens maak as jy ‘n veeboer is en jy wil jou veld oppas… V/O The amount of pesticide they use is staggering. Riaan says he uses about 10 to 12, 200 liter drums of chemicals per week! The pesticides are distributed from 2 depots in the Northern Cape - one in Upington, and the other one, here in De Aar. Willem Symington Claire: So when we’re talking about the actual pesticide, is it environmentally friendly, I mean we’re talking about 100s of liters being sprayed across the veld. Is it going to do any lasting damage, or no? Willem, In previous years when we still worked with organophosphates, that was really harmful to the environment, … but it’s new pesticide. It’s registered only for locusts, it’s very specie specific, it does no further harm to the environment… LINK It’s hard to imagine that right now there are millions of locusts swarming this part of the country. We’ve been here for 2 days and have traveled a thousand kilometres and have not spotted a single one yet. And that is why they are so difficult to control and with the veld looking this lush there could be a swarm just on the other side of this pond and no-one would notice. Riaan Badenhorst Baie boere is nie op die plase self nie. Daar’s niemand op die plase nie. 90% van die sprinkane wat gerapporteer word is op ‘n pad, so die ouens ry oor die sprinkane en dan sien hulle hul toevallig. V/o Our Locust hunting trip is fast coming to an end, but in a last-ditch attempt to see the hoppers, we head to Strydenburg where some locusts were spotted earlier today. But as luck would have it, we drive into a massive swarm on the road… UPSOUND CLAIRE We’ve got locusts! V/O But catching them is no easy task! UPSOUND CLAIRE Out of my hands! V/O Luckily we were forward thinking… CLAIRE LINK Guys I don’t know… I’ve been on a hunt for many things in my life but I feel like I’ve won the jackpot by finding these little locusts.. We’ve been looking for you for so long… These are tiny and we were just driving on the road and finally we saw millions of them… they look like dust… V/O In Strydenburg, local District Locust Officer, Johannes van der Merwe takes us to another swarm of newly hatched hoppers… Johannes van der Merwe Kyk hoe kom hulle af hierso in die pad… V/O We tell Johannes about the swarm we just encountered outside the town. If the rain stays away he will go look for them once the sun sets… Johannes van der Merwe Hier is duidelik ‘n krises aan die kom want hulle broei uit soos julle nou kan sien… Willem Symington Claire: Would you choose locusts over the drought? I will always use locusts over the drought because if the two have locusts, you have to have some rain, and the locust is not going to eat up all the grazing. Riaan Badenhorst Ons sal liewerste maar met hulle baklei voor ons weer ‘n droogte vat…. V/O The sun sets as we head back to Johannesburg … past the maize growing in dams of water … and one cannot help but wonder to what extent all this is because of OUR mistreatment of nature… ********* PROMO 1 21’ Claire Link: I’m in the Northern Cape and it’s like you’ve never seen it before. It’s green, it’s lush. For the most part the farmers are happy… except for one little problem.. Wait.. make that a million little problems. Upsound Willem: Overhead the sun darkens. Upsound Riaan: Dis nou een van die plae van die bybel nog wat regtig ‘n plaag is… PROMO 2 21” Millions of hoppers, munching their way through the Karoo veld… UPSOUND Willem: They eat everything… UPSOUND Riaan: As jy hulle moet los dan sal dit katastrofiese gevolge hê. UPSOUND Willem: Can you imagine what would happen of all these swarms goes into your crop growing areas… We travel to the Great Karoo in search of locusts… PROMO 3 11” UPSOUND: Day two of our road trip and it has not stopped raining! Wonderful for the farmers, but not so good for hunting locusts…

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Unprecedented rainfall across the country has brought not only relief for our farmers... but also millions of brown locusts!
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Swarms of brown locusts have been reported across the Eastern and Northern Cape - across the Karoo. And they're munching their way through farmers' crops and grazing. The swarms are said to travel up to 100kms in a single day and are massive, containing hundreds of thousands of individuals. Farmers speak of swarms that span a kilometre, eating EVERYTHING in sight. The Government is in charge of control, but because of the nature of the insecticide used, houses cannot be treated, so people are suffering. Dead locusts, left to rot are smelly and an eyesore in some smaller towns.
metadata.Summary: Farmers are crying, they have spent the last years battling a drought and now that they finally have grazing for their livestock, that could be wiped out overnight by a single swarm of brown locusts. And a bigger threat looms for the adjacent provinces. If the swarms migrate to our crop intensive areas (Northwest or Free State) they could have a massive impact on our food production and cause huge problems for the agricultural sector. On average we have large outbreaks in SA between 7 to 11 years. The locusts live for about 78 days and a single female lays 380 eggs. Problems we have these days is that the Karoo has changed over the last few decades. A lot of land is being farmed remotely, which means there is no-one on the land and there is a break in surveilance. Increased security on farms also means that pest control teams don’t have easy access to land…
metadata.Further information: The summer rains have wreaked havoc for farmers. 60% of crops in the Western Freestate are said to fail because of too much rain or hail. And it’s too late to replant. Same happening in Eastern Freestate where maize farmers are reporting fungus in their crops because the maize and wheat is literally standing in swamps. Also means farmers cannot get into the fields to remove weeds and do pest control. In some places wheat is ready to be harvested but they cannot get into the fields. According to the Agricultural Pests Act, Government is responsible for the management of Brown Locust outbreaks. And generally they do a good job, — the only thing farmers can do themselves is crush the hoppers before they fly. The locusts are high in fat and a good source of protein so sheep can feed on them, and technically humans too… but there are too many locusts and too few people to control the outbreak. Biggest problem we have is monitoring the swarms. They can travel up to 100km a day. UN Food and Agriculture Organisation has a good model where they track pests with satellite technology and drones. We should have something similar, but we don’t. The Karoo Brown Locust is a medium-sized insect from the genus Locustana. It is native to the arid Karoo and especially adapted for this dry region. Eggs have an impermeable cuticle to protect them and they can lie in the ground, unhatched for years… waiting for the conditions to be perfect! According to records, there are outbreaks reported as far back as 1797… and 2022 seems to be their lucky year! Swarms have been reported across the Eastern and Northern Cape - across the Karoo. The last major outbreak was in 1985-86 and ended up costing the country about R50 million. It takes a lot of labour and costly chemicals to destroy a swarm. Agri chemical and -pest specialist, Dr Gerhard Verdoorn says at the moment the Karoo vegetation is quite abundant thanks to the rains. This means that the veld is full of food for the critters. But they cannot be left… They could move to other areas in the country where they can do a lot more damage and they do pose a threat to road safety. When you drive through a swarm your windscreen will be covered in a thick fatty goo — making visibility difficult, which could cause problems, especially on smaller roads.
